tagline: Stage stops, sheep research and an opal town in Clark County
intro: Dubois stands at 5,148 feet above sea level near the Caribou-Targhee National Forest. To the north, the Bitterroot Range forms Clark County’s boundary with Montana and the continental divide.

In 1864, stagecoach stops at Dry Creek and Beaver Canyon served the route between Salt Lake City and Montana mining towns. The Utah and Northern Railway reached Beaver Canyon in 1879; that settlement moved to Spencer in 1897.

In Dubois, the former St. James’ Episcopal Mission Church carries the name Heritage Hall Museum. Six miles north of town is the U.S. Sheep Experiment Station. Spencer serves as a base for an opal mine five to six miles outside town.

moments.title: Dubois
moments.text: Dry Creek, now Dubois, had a stagecoach stop established in 1864 on the route between Salt Lake City and the Montana mining towns. Dry Creek became Dubois in 1892, taking the name of Idaho politician Fred Dubois. On Reynolds Street, St. James’ Episcopal Mission Church was built in 1904 to a design by Wayland & Fennell. Its Gothic Revival design has a gable facing the front. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1993, the building was renamed Heritage Hall Museum in 2017.
moments.notice: The former mission church has a front-facing gable and Gothic Revival design.

moments.title: U.S. Sheep Experiment Station
moments.text: Sheep breeding and rangeland research share a home at the U.S. Sheep Experiment Station, run by the USDA’s Agricultural Research Service. The Columbia breed’s originating flock moved here in 1918 after early crosses in Wyoming. The station also developed the Polypay in the 1960s and the Targhee, a rangeland breed named for the adjacent national forest. Its lands include subalpine meadows, foothills, sagebrush steppe and desert shrubland. Research ranges from reproductive efficiency and breed improvement to grazing management and the quality of meat and wool. Land in Montana’s Centennial Mountains and near Kilgore supports seasonal grazing and rangeland studies.

moments.title: Spencer
moments.text: Spencer is the base for Idaho’s opal mine, with the mine itself five to six miles outside the hamlet. Its settlement history includes a move: Beaver Canyon relocated to Spencer in 1897, after the Utah and Northern Railway had reached Beaver Canyon in 1879. Spencer incorporated in 1947. The 2020 census counted 31 residents.
